name: PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sumber Global Energy - a coal trader priced as if the cycle never turned
frontmatter.summary: SGER buys and resells Indonesian thermal coal and is diversifying into nickel, sand and limestone, petroleum coke and energy-transition products. Revenue halved in FY2025 as the coal price normalised and the Vietnamese export book collapsed, and operating cash flow went negative. The shares have tripled to a record and now embed a recovery far beyond what a trading book can earn at through-cycle prices. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: SGER earns a trading spread, not a mining margin: the FY2025 cost of revenues moved almost exactly with revenue, and the coal gross spread has run between mid-single and mid-teens percent, so group profit is a function of tonnes, price level and working-capital funding, not of a reserve base.

The market capitalisation is about IDR13,093.0bn, roughly thirty times our through-cycle EBITDA, after a share-price run from Rp240 to Rp840; the price implies a Newcastle price of about US$167/t, well above the level at which marginal Indonesian supply clears.

Our going-concern DCF at the desk through-cycle Newcastle path, with realisation calibrated on the company own disclosed actuals and a terminal value at the rupiah long-run rate, produces Rp113 a share; the no-terminal-value life-of-asset frame the industry card mandates for coal producers gives Rp58, its floor, against today Rp840.

The FY2025 collapse is not only price: a quality dispute with a Vietnamese buyer [S17] sits behind the loss of the two customers that supplied a third of FY2024 revenue [S18], and the board declared no dividend for the year [S0].
We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp94, -88.6% against the last close; even the bull case, on a higher coal price and a wider book, leaves the shares far below the market price.

catalysts.event: Series A bond repaid at maturity from internal cash, leaving only the smaller Series B outstanding
H1 FY2026 results reported, with revenue, net profit and the coal segment result all disclosed
Government RKAB output quota for 2027 to be settled after the industry proposed a lower ceiling
FY2026 audited results and the AGM dividend decision for the year

blocks.text: SGER is a coal trader with a mining side-show. It buys thermal coal from Indonesian concession holders and resells it, mostly for export, alongside a fast-growing set of non-coal commodity lines: nickel ore, oil palm products, sand and limestone, and petroleum coke [S3]. Coal was IDR4,940.4bn of the IDR6,739.5bn of FY2025 net revenue, but the non-coal lines have gone from almost nothing to a IDR836.6bn nickel business and similar-sized sand and limestone and petroleum coke lines within two years, and management is now building a hydrogen-peroxide plant at Merak and a wood-pellet export business as the post-coal growth engine [S3, S10].

That diversification is real but it is not yet large enough to matter against the price of the shares. The company's economics are a trading spread: in FY2025 cost of revenues fell by almost exactly the same percentage as revenue [S2], which is what a bought-in product looks like, not a mine plan. Group gross margin was single-digit percent in FY2025, and the coal line alone earned IDR4,940.4bn of revenue against IDR4,538.5bn of cost, an eight percent spread [S3]. On a book of 4.6 Mt at through-cycle prices that spread supports an EBITDA of roughly IDR398.7bn, an EBITDA margin in the low single digits — and that is the whole of the profit pool.

The market, however, is paying IDR13,093.0bn for the equity. The shares have run from Rp240 to a record Rp840 on the coal-price spike, the diversification story and a bonus-share and treasury-share programme, and the last close sits at the top of the fifty-two week range [S0]. On our numbers the company earns IDR171.7bn in FY2026E, so the market is applying an earnings multiple in the tens to a business whose FY2025 profit was hit by the collapse of its coal exports and whose operating cash flow was negative [S3].

We value SGER on two discounted cash-flow runs plus two cross-checks, all at the coal desk's through-cycle Newcastle path with the realisation calibrated on the years for which SGER has itself disclosed traded tonnage. The industry card's primary for coal is a life-of-asset DCF run with no terminal value — the right frame for a depleting producer, and a deliberate floor here — and it gives Rp58 a share. Because SGER owns no depleting mine (its only mining is the Tujuh Bara Sejahtera operation [S18, F22]) and its nickel, sand-and-limestone, petroleum-coke and hydrogen-peroxide lines are a growing going concern [S3, S10, S16], we also run a going-concern DCF with a terminal value at the rupiah long-run rate, which gives Rp113. The two cross-checks — EV/EBITDA at the blended peer-and-own-history multiple, and dividend capacity — sit at Rp59 and Rp36. Blending the four methods at our revised weights gives a base value of Rp85; weighting the scenarios by their probabilities gives a target of Rp94, which is -88.6% against the last close. We initiate at **SELL**.

A commodity trader's reported profit is a thin spread multiplied by a large turnover, so the
level of the share price, not the direction of the commodity, is normally the swing factor in
its valuation. Traders rarely own the reserve; they own relationships, working capital and
shipping. That makes them sensitive to supplier concentration and to the cost of funding the
advance book, and it makes their margins mean-revert faster than a producer's.

What would change our mind, in order of importance: a credible, funded expansion of the non-coal businesses to a scale at which they carry the group's earnings; evidence that the coal book can be rebuilt to the volumes of the middle of the decade at a normal spread; and a share price that stops discounting both. The reverse DCF says the price needs a coal price of about US$167/t, roughly 1.4 times the desk's FY2027E benchmark of US$118/t and well above its long-run marker of US$105/t, to be justified on the coal business alone [S23].

PT Sumber Global Energy Tbk was established in 2008 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2020. Its stated line of business is wholesale trading in solid, liquid and gaseous fuels and, through its subsidiaries, new and renewable energy; in practice the group is a merchant of Indonesian thermal coal and, increasingly, of other bulk commodities [S2]. It is headquartered in Jakarta, runs marketing offices in Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, and lists mining operational areas in East Kalimantan, South Kalimantan, Jambi, Central Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi [S2]. The workforce is small — the annual report and the FY2025 accounts both describe a company in the tens of direct employees, though the two documents give different counts, so we rely on the payroll cost rather than the headcount [S2, S3] — which is what a trading model looks like on the payroll.

Revenue splits cleanly into coal and everything else. In FY2025 coal contributed IDR4,940.4bn of the IDR6,739.5bn total; nickel IDR836.6bn; oil palm products IDR497.6bn; sand and limestone IDR285.6bn; and petroleum coke IDR179.4bn [S3]. Two years earlier the non-coal lines were immaterial: FY2023 coal revenue was IDR12,217.6bn against a total of IDR12,312.9bn, with nickel at only a token amount [S18]. The shift is partly deliberate diversification and partly the collapse of the coal book, and both are visible in the same table.

The coal business is a pure intermediation model. SGER contracts with concession holders — the FY2025 accounts list sale-and-purchase agreements with PT Niaga Trada Nusantara, PT Niaga Bara Karya, PT Merge Mining Industri and others, and with suppliers including PT Batuah Energi Prima [S3] — and on-sells to export customers under either open tender, usually in consortium with local partners, or direct repeat orders [S13]. Its historic market was Vietnam: it supplied a Vietnam power plant under a 2,500,000 MT contract with Viet Phat Import Export Trading Investment JSC [S14], took a 500,000 MT order from VIMC Shipping Company through its Dubai subsidiary Hineni Seven Resources [S11], and signed consortium contracts with Coalimex and Vinacomin Northern Coal [S8, S12]. Other export destinations named by management include China, India, the Philippines, Malaysia and Bangladesh [S11].

The mining side is real but small. Through an operational-cooperation agreement signed in July 2024 and amended twice, SGER funds and operates the mining, haulage and sale of coal inside PT Tujuh Bara Sejahtera's production IUP, with SGER providing the working capital and taking the sale proceeds, and PT Tujuh Bara Sejahtera guaranteeing a coal quantity of 2,000,000 MT at a cumulative stripping ratio of 7 while retaining a small annual offtake quota [S18]. SGER does not describe a reserve base of its own, and the annual report's operating review does not disclose reserves [S2, S3].

Indonesian thermal-coal merchants sit between thousands of small concession holders and the
seaborne buyers. Their edge is logistics and receivables financing as much as price: they
provide advances to suppliers who cannot fund their own working capital, and they carry the
letter-of-credit and inspection risk on the way out. That is why their balance sheets look
like a bank's and their income statements look like a wholesaler's.

On market position the company is a challenger. It is a mid-sized trader, not an integrated producer: the group produced no coal of its own before the 2024 cooperation agreement, and its FY2023 traded volume of 10.0 Mt is a fraction of the volumes moved by the large producers on the same exchange [S13]. Its differentiator has been Vietnam and, before the FY2025 rupture, two customers that each accounted for more than a tenth of group revenue — Viet Phat at one-fifth and Vietnam Ocean Shipping at more than an eighth of FY2024 revenue [S18]. Concentration of that scale in a trading business is a structural vulnerability, and it materialised: SGER's FY2025 coal revenue fell to IDR4,940.4bn from IDR14,209.1bn [S3, S18].

The controlling shareholder is PT Sumbermas Inti Energi with 50.08% of the shares; directors Vivi Ramalyati Hutama and Welly Thomas hold further stakes and the public holds the balance [S2]. The group structure includes Hineni Seven Resources DMCC in the UAE, the Singapore marketing arm, a coal-trading subsidiary, and a hydrogen-peroxide venture [S3, S11]. Welly Thomas is president director and Michael Harold is corporate secretary [S2, S6].

Seaborne thermal coal is a large, mature, politically contested market in which Indonesia is the largest exporter, and the current cycle is being driven by three things: an Asian demand base that has not yet rolled over, a Chinese supply and import policy that swings the balance every quarter, and an Indonesian output regime that is now being actively managed [S19, S20, S21].

The price tape tells the story. Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg NAR averaged US$136/t in calendar 2024 and US$108/t in calendar 2025 in the World Bank's Pink Sheet, down from a much higher level in the preceding spike, and has since firmed through 2026, with mid-year quarterly assessments well above the annual averages of the prior two years and the latest monthly prints near the highs of the period [S23]. The coal desk's deck carries US$137/t for FY2026E and US$118/t for FY2027E before mean reversion toward a long-run marker around US$105/t [S23]. Spot sits well above the forward path [S23], which the desk reads as the war-premium carry rather than a new level.

Indonesian policy is now the swing factor on the supply side. The government sets annual output quotas through the RKAB approvals, and after a record year the 2026 quota was cut for price-management reasons; the industry association has proposed a lower ceiling again for 2027 to hold the price up [S19, S21, S22]. Regulators have also moved the reference-price machinery: the HBA is set twice monthly and the latest high-calorific print is US$127/t, with the current decree used as the pricing floor for exports [S24, S25]. For a trader of mid-rank Indonesian coal, those decrees and the RKAB quota are the policy variables that matter most.

The HBA is a grade ladder, not a single number, and SGER's tonnes sit on the upper rungs of it. The reference price is set by calorific value: the 5,300 kcal/kg GAR grade (HBA I) prints US$93.6/t and the 4,100 kcal/kg grade (HBA II) prints US$66.1/t, with the 3,400 kcal/kg grade (HBA III) at US$45.5/t [S25]. SGER's stated product is a mid-rank thermal coal of about 4,800 kcal/kg GAR [S13], which clears between HBA II and HBA I — it is above the 4,100 kcal/kg grade, not in the HBA III tranche (the 3,400 kcal/kg bucket). Our FY2026E realised price of 65.8 USD/t is therefore set below the mid-point of the two rungs its grade actually straddles, and sits just under the HBA II print [S25]. The model prices the tonnes off the desk's Newcastle series because that is the only coal series the deck carries a forecast path for, but the realisation ratio is calibrated on SGER's own disclosed cargoes [S13, S17, S18], and the resulting realised level is consistent with — indeed slightly conservative against — the HBA ladder for its grade.

Demand is the firmer leg. Chinese import demand has been volatile but large, India has repeatedly faced generation shortfalls that push it back into the seaborne market, and Vietnamese and Bangladeshi power additions have created new buyers on Indonesia's doorstep [S20]. The coal desk's own reading is that Indonesian output runs near the quota level, that Chinese mines restart through FY2027, and that the war premium decays gradually rather than snapping — which is what the FY2027E step-down in the deck reflects [S23].

Competitive structure is unattractive. Thermal coal is a commodity with no product differentiation, buyers run competitive tenders that explicitly require local partners, and the large integrated producers have their own logistics, lower cost bases and long-term offtake [S13]. The five forces are as expected: low supplier power in aggregate but high supplier counterparty risk, powerful concentrated buyers on the other side, a permanent threat of substitution from renewables in the long run and from competing exporters in the short run, and rivalry that expresses itself as margin compression rather than price wars. SGER's position in that structure is honest but unremarkable: it competes on reach, financing and reliability rather than on cost or scale, and it has no reserve moat [S13].

Coal trading margins in the region are typically a few dollars a tonne, and they depend as much
on the cost of carrying inventory and advances as on the headline spread. When prices fall
quickly, traders with long advance books can be squeezed twice — the spread narrows and the
working capital does not release. That asymmetry, rather than the coal price itself, is the
recurring cause of distress in the sector.

The relevant external influences for SGER are therefore the Newcastle and HBA price paths (the desk's newc and hba series); the rupiah, because costs are dollar-denominated and the reporting currency is rupiah [S0]; Indonesian quota policy through the RKAB cycle [S19, S22]; and the cost of the working capital that funds the advance book, currently priced off rupiah bonds and bank lines [S6]. Each of those is treated as a driver in the model, not as background.

SGER's five-year history is a cycle in miniature. Revenue ran IDR10,448.9bn, IDR12,312.9bn and IDR14,762.5bn in FY2022A to FY2024A, then collapsed to IDR6,739.5bn in FY2025A as the coal price normalised and the export book broke [S2, S3]. Net profit attributable to shareholders followed the same shape — IDR687.9bn, IDR658.7bn, then IDR213.3bn [S0] — because the cost base did not fall as fast as revenue at the margin, and because the interest bill rose sharply as debt funded the inventory [S3].

Revenue build. The model builds coal revenue as traded volume times realised price, where the realised price is a calibrated ratio to the Newcastle benchmark. That ratio, 0.48, is set from the FY2023 actuals, the last year in which the company disclosed both a tonnage and a segment revenue: IDR12,217.6bn on 10.0 Mt [S13, S18], against a benchmark that averaged far higher that year [S23]. The same ratio is consistent with SGER's own export contract prices in 2024 and 2025 [S11, S17]. Volume in FY2026E is 4.6 Mt, anchored on the coal segment revenue of IDR3,160.0bn that the company reported for the first half. We convert that at the calibrated realisation and the deck's rupiah and apply the historical first-half share of the year — the first half carried about three-fifths of FY2025, when H1 revenue of IDR4,050.0bn stood against a full year of IDR6,739.5bn [S2, S6] — which anchors the full year at 4.6 Mt rather than the larger number a second-half recovery would imply. No such recovery is sourced, so we assume none; the growth thereafter comes only from the rebuilt export book, not from a return to the FY2024 volume.

Margins and costs. The gross margin is a spread, and we hold the last actual's spread. FY2025 coal revenue of IDR4,940.4bn against coal cost of revenues of IDR4,538.5bn is an eight percent spread on the coal line, and the non-coal lines earned a similar one [S3]. The model therefore carries procurement cost at 60.5 USD/t in FY2026E, roughly ninety-two percent of the realised selling price, and lets it move with the benchmark rather than holding it flat in real terms — the drift is justified in the engine's quality gate because the FY2025 accounts show cost of revenues falling by almost the same percentage as revenue [S2]. SG&A is held at a little over two percent of revenue, the H1 FY2026 ratio, rather than the inflated FY2025 ratio, because the absolute cost base is roughly fixed and the headcount is small [S0, S2].

Cash flow and working capital. This is where the trading model bites. FY2025 operating cash flow was negative IDR197.4bn, the third consecutive year of cash absorption, and total advances to suppliers, projects and others stood at IDR3,475.7bn at the balance-sheet date, a sum equal to more than half of that year's revenue [S3]. The audit report identifies revenue recognition on coal trading and the measurement of those advances as its key audit matters, which is the correct place for the scepticism to sit [S3]. Receivables are small by comparison — IDR364.5bn of coal-trading receivables — so the working capital is upstream, in prepayments to suppliers, not downstream.

Balance sheet and debt. Gross debt was about IDR2,300.7bn at the FY2025 balance-sheet date, with net debt of about IDR1,939.4bn, and the group carries rupiah bonds at ten to eleven percent coupons [S3, S6]. Since then the larger Series A bond has been repaid from internal cash, leaving only the smaller Series B outstanding to October 2027 [S6, S10]. Equity is IDR2,233.9bn and D&A is small — IDR475.4bn of fixed-asset additions in FY2025 was mostly growth, against a depreciation charge of IDR17.7bn — because the mining assets the group has capitalised are still classified as mines under development and are not yet depreciated [S2, S3].

Capital allocation. SGER has historically distributed a meaningful share of earnings, but the record has been cut back hard: cash dividends paid were IDR140.3bn in FY2025, against a share-dividend and cash-dividend combination the year before, and no dividend has been declared for FY2025 [S0, S3]. With operating cash flow negative and the advance book still large, we assume a partial resumption at a payout well below the historical average, funded from earnings rather than from debt [S0].

Earnings-quality flags. Running the house screen: the three-year accruals ratio is comfortably above the ten percent threshold, because net profit has persistently outrun cash, and the trend is not improving — the gap is driven by negative operating cash flow against positive accounting profit [S3]. The divergence flags are present in the classic form: advances to suppliers grew while revenue fell, and the FY2025 margin contraction came with a collapse in cash conversion [S3]. On the IDX regime flags, we find no special-monitoring-board status or special notation, the audit opinion for FY2025 is unqualified, and the auditor is an established firm [S3]. Related-party flows we quantify rather than wave away: related-party other payables of IDR169.9bn at the FY2025 balance-sheet date are 5.2% of total liabilities and are owed to the shareholders of subsidiaries, with no related-party revenue or purchases disclosed [S3]. The supplier-advance book — the audit report's other key matter — is not a related-party channel: the accounts state the significant portion of the advances is to third parties for coal and nickel purchases, IDR3,301.1bn of the IDR3,475.7bn total [S3]. One flag is qualitative and important: the Vietnamese trade ministry has alleged that a cargo certified at a higher calorific value was delivered at a materially lower one, and the company disputes it [S17]. We classify that as an allegation of grade misrepresentation, not a manipulation-class finding on revenue or cash: the discount, if any, belongs in the pre-mortem and in the supplier- relationship risk, not in an auto-pass.

A trading company's accruals ratio is a blunt instrument, because prepayments to suppliers sit
in working capital rather than in the income statement and can look like a permanent feature of
the model. The test is whether the advances convert into delivered tonnes within the contract
cycle. Where they do, low cash conversion is a growth cost; where they do not, it is the
classic signature of earnings that do not exist.

A coal trader should not be valued on its current-year multiple. The house method card for commodity cyclicals is explicit that NAV is built from life-of-asset cash flows at through-cycle prices, minus net debt and capitalised corporate costs, and that spot earnings are a cycle position, not a value. That fits SGER awkwardly — it owns almost no depleting asset, and the card's primary engine for coal is the no-terminal-value life-of-asset DCF that the industry configuration sets for every COAL name — so we run that engine as the mandated primary and as a floor, and value the going concern the company actually is alongside it. What the group converts into cash over a full cycle, at a normal spread and a normal price, is the value, and one war-premium year is not that.

We therefore run two DCFs at a WACC of 11.2%: the no-terminal-value life-of-asset run that the card mandates for coal, which gives Rp58 a share and carries 20.0% of the blend as the depleting-asset floor; and a going-concern DCF with a terminal value at the rupiah long-run growth rate of 3.5%, which gives Rp113 and carries 40.0%. The terminal value is about 22.4% of the going-concern value, and its absence from the life-of-asset run is precisely the understatement a no-terminal-value frame imposes on a merchant whose franchise outlives its coal book — we weight the going-concern run above the floor for that reason, and we state the understatement rather than hide it. Two cross-checks are run at the industry weights: EV/EBITDA at 9.6 times, the average of the peer median and SGER's own five-year average, which gives Rp59; and dividend capacity, which gives Rp36. Blending the four gives a base value of Rp85.

The WACC build is unremarkable except for where the risk sits. The risk-free rate is the Indonesian government curve, the equity risk premium and country risk premium are the house inputs, and the unlevered beta is the industry median from our own regressions. Leverage is modest at 14.5% of capital, but the cost of debt used in the WACC is high: the house build — the rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate debt spread, not a company rate — puts it at 9.4% pre-tax, close to the ten-percent-plus coupons on SGER's own bonds [S6]. That market rate is distinct from the rate the model charges on the profit and loss: the interest line runs off the company's own effective rate of 8.5% on opening debt — FY2025 interest expense over average gross debt [S3] — so the WACC uses the market build and the operating forecast uses the actual rate. The cost of equity lands at 11.9% and the WACC at 11.2%.

The DCF is a spread business discounted: the cash flow is thin because the spread is thin and because revenue growth pulls working capital into the advance book, and the value is therefore highly geared to the coal price and to the spread on it. That gearing is exactly why the cross-checks do not agree. EV/EBITDA, which capitalises the FY2025 trough EBITDA at a historical multiple, gives a different answer from the DCF because the multiple is itself derived from a period when the market capitalised higher earnings; 2.3% against the primary is the divergence in the set and we discuss it rather than smoothing it. The dividend cross-check comes in below the primary because our assumed payout is far under the historical record [S0, S3].

We test the two drivers that matter. Benchmark coal price and the rupiah move the value together, since the realised price translates at the prevailing rate; volume and cost intensity move it in opposite directions. The sensitivity grid shows what the model's structure already implies — that the value is roughly linear in the coal price over the range tested, and that no plausible combination of volume and cost intensity gets the shares to today's price.

What today's price implies is the more useful question. Running the reverse DCF, the market price of Rp840 requires a Newcastle benchmark of about US$167/t, roughly 1.4 times the desk's FY2027E benchmark of US$118/t and well above both its long-run marker of US$105/t and the level at which Indonesian marginal supply has historically cleared [S23]. Put differently, the market is capitalising the group at IDR13,093.0bn against a through-cycle EBITDA in the hundreds of billions of rupiah — a multiple in the high twenties — for a business whose FY2025 operating cash flow was negative [S3]. That is the core of our variant view, and we can source it rather than assert it. The industry card tells us to respect a name that re-rates with the complex, and to re-set the through-cycle marker and re-test the view when the complex moves; we do both. The marker here is the desk's through-cycle price path, not today's tape — the model runs on the deck's forecast series falling toward a long-run US$105/t, not on spot US$150/t [S23] — and the rating is tested against that re-set marker, where our target of Rp94 sits against a market price of Rp840. What the card's first-step rule assumes, and what SGER does not have, is a profit and loss geared to the complex. SGER's coal gross spread has sat in a narrow band through the whole price cycle: coal revenue of IDR12,217.6bn against a coal cost of revenues of IDR11,170.4bn in FY2023 [S18], IDR14,209.1bn against IDR13,225.9bn in FY2024 [S18], and IDR4,940.4bn against IDR4,538.5bn in FY2025 [S3] — a spread that has stayed in the high-single-digit percent range while the Newcastle benchmark fell from its spike toward the level the desk now carries [S23]. A wholesale trader's spread is a pass-through service fee on a bought-in tonne, set by logistics and financing rather than by the level of the commodity, so it does not widen when the benchmark re-rates; a complex re-rating is alpha for the producer who owns the reserve, not for the merchant who intermediates it. That is why the SELL survives the re-set marker, and not merely the taper: even on the desk's through-cycle path and with the going-concern franchise valued, the target is a fraction of the market price.

Scenario probability weighting lifts the target from the base value of Rp85 to Rp94, because the bull case is worth far more than the base case is worth more than the bear case — the convexity of a levered spread business. Even the bull case, at Rp189, sits far below the market price.
Downside risks, with our assessment of likelihood and impact.

Regulatory and policy — medium likelihood, high impact. Indonesian coal policy is being used actively to manage price: the RKAB quota has been cut, the industry has proposed a lower ceiling again for 2027, and the HBA decree now operates as an export pricing floor [S19, S21, S22, S24]. For a merchant, a quota cut that shrinks the pool of coal available to buy is a volume risk, and a rising domestic-market obligation is a mix risk. SGER reports no domestic obligation share, so the cap driver is inert in our model, but that is an assumption, not a fact [S13].

Commodity price — high likelihood, high impact. The desk already assumes the war premium decays from spot toward a long-run marker [S23]. Because SGER's margin is roughly proportional to its selling price, a price normalisation compresses profit twice: the spread narrows and the inventory carried against it devalues.

Concentration and counterparty — medium likelihood, high impact. The company's FY2024 was made by two Vietnamese customers, each above a tenth of revenue [S18]; both are gone from the FY2025 disclosures. The quality dispute with a Vietnamese buyer remains unresolved [S17]. Rebuilding an export book means new counterparties, new inspection risk and new advance exposure.

Operational and company-specific — medium likelihood, high impact. Working capital is the operational risk: IDR3,475.7bn of advances to suppliers, projects and others at the last balance-sheet date, negative operating cash flow, and an audit report that makes the measurement of those advances and of coal-trading revenue its key audit matters [S3]. We quantify the related-party exposure the earnings screen requires: related-party other payables were IDR169.9bn, or 5.2% of total liabilities, with no related-party revenue or purchases disclosed [S3]; and the advance book is stated to be to third parties for coal and nickel purchases — IDR3,301.1bn of the IDR3,475.7bn total [S3] — so the related-party channel is not where the risk sits. The risk is plain counterparty non-conversion against an advance book equal to more than half of FY2025 revenue. Our scenarios do not model a write-down because no default is disclosed, but this is where the equity is at risk: a single large advance that failed to convert would be a loss against an equity base of IDR2,233.9bn [S3], so a write-down of even a fraction of the book would take a material part of book value, and it would hit in the same year that the spread is under pressure. The signpost is the conversion of the balance into delivered tonnes.

Governance — medium likelihood, medium impact. The controlling shareholder holds 50.08%, the free float is thin, the shares have tripled, and the market's liquidity in the name is modest relative to the capitalisation [S0, S2]. Minority interests have little leverage over capital allocation.

Funding and liquidity — low-to-medium likelihood, medium impact. The near-term bond wall has been cleared with the Series A repayment [S6, S10], but the blended cost of debt is high and the group depends on bank lines to fund the advance book [S3, S6].
Currency — medium likelihood, medium impact. Costs are dollar-denominated, reporting is in rupiah, and the macro desk expects the rupiah to weaken on current-account pressure [S0].

Our bear case assumes the coal price gives back the war premium faster than the desk implies, on a slightly smaller book and a procurement cost that does not fall quite as fast, and it also cuts the non-coal lines — the nickel, sand and limestone, petroleum coke, hydrogen-peroxide and wood-pellet businesses — to four-fifths of our forecast revenue. The bull case assumes the price holds and Indonesia's quota discipline keeps seaborne supply tight, so SGER trades a larger book at a wider spread, and it carries the stated bull driver explicitly: the non-coal lines scale to a fifth above our forecast revenue as well as the wider coal spread. Both cases shock the same four drivers — the coal benchmark, volume, unit cost and non-coal revenue — by mirrored amounts; the asymmetry in the resulting values is the convexity of the business, not an asymmetric assumption set.

Signposts that would change the view: first, quarterly coal segment revenue and the disclosed tonnage trend — if the company begins disclosing volumes again and they are growing, our revenue build is too low; second, the split between coal and non-coal revenue and the margin the non-coal lines earn, because that is the only route to a larger profit pool at a smaller coal book; third, RKAB outcomes and any change to the domestic-market obligation regime; fourth, the resolution of the Vietnamese dispute and any provision taken; and fifth, the cash-conversion trend, which is the single best test of whether the reported spread is real.

Ownership and control sit with PT Sumbermas Inti Energi at 50.08%, with two individuals holding further blocks and the public the remainder; the free float is roughly 30.5% of the register but the market's three-month turnover is modest relative to the capitalisation [S0, S2]. There is no dual-class structure and no VIE: this is a straightforward Indonesian listed trading company, and the governance question is not opacity of structure but the concentration of control and the thin float.

The board and management are stable and small. Welly Thomas has been president director through the expansion and the FY2025 contraction, Michael Harold is corporate secretary, and the company reports its internal audit function and audit committee [S2, S6]. The FY2025 consolidated accounts were audited by Morhan & Rekan, which issued an unqualified opinion [S3]. There is no auditor down-tier change or qualification to flag in the period we reviewed.

Related-party dealings are modest by the standards of the market: related-party other payables of the same order as third-party trade payables, with trade payables reported wholly against third parties [S3]. The company's substantial transactions — supplier advances, sale-and- purchase agreements, the operational-cooperation agreement — are disclosed in the notes, which is where they should be [S3, S18]. We found no evidence of sales routed through an affiliate at non-market terms in the disclosures we reviewed, and we state that as an observation about what is disclosed rather than an assurance about what exists.

The governance flag we do carry forward is the Vietnamese quality dispute. Vietnam's ministry of industry and trade wrote to Indonesia's energy minister alleging that a cargo contracted at one calorific specification arrived materially below it, causing the buyer penalties, and the company has publicly disputed the account [S17]. The matter has been referred toward civil channels. We treat this as an allegation, and we discount it in the estimates in two places: the supplier and customer relationships that must be rebuilt to grow the book, and the pre-mortem on why the FY2025 collapse was worse than a price move alone would explain.

The dividend record is short and has now been interrupted. Cash dividends were paid in each of the last several years — the FY2025 payment of IDR140.3bn related to the prior year's earnings — but no dividend has been declared for FY2025, and the company instead repaid its maturing bond from cash [S0, S3, S6]. Minority income sits in the accounts as a small charge and the group has issued shares in subsidiaries to non-controlling interests, so the structure is not a single clean subsidiary tree [S3].

ESG exposures are the sector's standard ones. Scope one and scope two emissions are immaterial at the group's own small operational footprint, but the product is thermal coal and the group's revenue is overwhelmingly carbon-intensive by nature, which is a financing and reputational exposure rather than a physical one [S2]. The company frames its transition strategy around renewables, wood pellets and the hydrogen-peroxide project [S2, S10]. Health and safety disclosure is thin, consistent with a business that employs few people directly and contracts its operational work to licensed mining-services holders [S3, S18].

For coal merchants, ESG risk is transmitted mainly through banking relationships and export
credit rather than through carbon pricing, because the coal is burned somewhere else. The
practical test for an investor is whether the company's bank lines and trade-finance limits
are being renewed on normal terms, which shows up in the cost of debt and the size of the
facilities rather than in a sustainability report.

The near-term calendar is quiet on the corporate side. The bond maturity that dominated the last year has passed [S6, S10], the first-half results are out [S16], and the next scheduled items are the 2027 quota decision [S22] and the FY2026 audit and dividend resolution [S3, S0].

blocks.text: The KPIs we will monitor between formal updates, in order of diagnostic value, are: coal tonnes and the coal-versus-non-coal revenue split, since the company publishes the latter but not the former [S3, S16]; the realised spread implied by segment revenue against segment cost of revenues [S3]; the size of the supplier advance balance and its conversion into delivered tonnes [S3]; operating cash flow against reported profit [S3]; gross and net debt and the cost of it [S3, S6]; and any announcement that reinstates volume disclosure, which would remove the largest single gap in our evidence base [S13].

bear.narrative: Coal normalises faster than the deck assumes and the traded book keeps shrinking: Newcastle gives back the war premium, SGER's procurement cost follows it down but not fast enough, the group is left with a thin spread on a smaller book while working capital stays locked in supplier advances, and the non-coal lines (nickel, sand & limestone, hydrogen peroxide, wood pellets) scale more slowly than we forecast.

bull.narrative: The war premium holds and Indonesia's RKAB discipline keeps seaborne thermal coal tight, so SGER trades a larger book at a wider spread, and the non-coal lines (nickel, sand & limestone, hydrogen peroxide, wood pellets) scale faster than we assume.

assumptions.label: Coal sales volume
assumptions.basis: Coal traded, Mt. FY2022A 7.5 Mt and FY2023A 10.0 Mt are the company's last disclosed tonnages [S13]; the traded book then grew with the Vietnam exports (Viet Phat 20.15% and Vietnam Ocean Shipping 13.39% of FY2024 revenue [S18]) before collapsing after the Dodec/Danka quality dispute [S17]. The company discloses no tonnage for FY2024, FY2025 or H1-2026, so FY2026E is anchored on the H1-2026 coal revenue of Rp3.16tn [S16] converted at the calibrated realisation and FY2026E FX, giving about 2.7 Mt in the half; the historical first-half share of the year is 60% (H1-2025 revenue Rp4.05tn of FY2025 Rp6.74tn [S2, S6]), so the anchored full year is about 4.6 Mt, and no second-half recovery above that split is sourced. It then grows gently with the rebuilt export book (Coalimex, VIMC, the Bangladesh enquiry) and never returns to the FY2024 peak, because the two Vietnamese buyers that drove that year are gone [S17, S18].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last year with BOTH a disclosed tonnage and revenue, then cross-checked on SGER's own contract prices: FY2023 coal revenue Rp12,217.6bn [S18] on 10.0 Mt [S13] = Rp1,221,765/t = US$80.2/t against the FY2023 Newcastle (6,000 kcal/kg NAR) average of US$172.8/t in the World Bank Pink Sheet [S23] = 0.46; SGER's Jun-2024 export cargo of NAR 4,500 went at US$66.7/t against Newcastle then near US$136 = 0.49 [S17]; its Mar-2025 cargo at US$71.4/t [S11]. SGER trades low-rank Indonesian thermal coal (34-53 GAR, typically 48GAR 4,800 kcal/kg [S13]), so a realisation near half of Newcastle is structural, not a haircut.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: SGER exports its traded tonnes (Vietnam, China, India, Bangladesh, Philippines, Malaysia [S11]); no domestic DMO-offtake share is disclosed in the LK, so the cap driver is inert.

assumptions.label: Cost intensity factor (bcm per tonne equivalent)
assumptions.basis: Used as a cost-intensity factor of 1.0, not a mining strip ratio: SGER buys and resells coal, so cost_per_bcm carries the delivered procurement cost per tonne directly. The only mining strip ratio in the group is the KSO's cumulative SR 7 over PT Tujuh Bara Sejahtera's IUP OP (2.0 Mt guaranteed) [S18], which is not the driver of a 6 Mt trading book.

assumptions.label: Delivered coal procurement cost per tonne (USD/t)
assumptions.basis: The price SGER pays its suppliers, which is the coal market price: the forecast series holds the FY2025 realised unit margin at ~8% of ASP (FY2025 coal cost of revenues Rp4,538.5bn on Rp4,940.4bn of coal revenue = 8.1%) so that the cost tracks the deck rather than staying flat while the benchmark moves. The LK shows cost and revenue moving together (cost of revenues -54.80% against revenues -54.35% in FY2025) [S2, S3, S18].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Set to zero: the cost base is bought-in coal, not diesel burned in a pit, so the brent link (d.oil.brent) is inert. Barging diesel is inside the delivered procurement price.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per tonne
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, barging, port handling and inspection are all inside the delivered procurement cost of a bought-in tonne; the FY2025 cost-of-revenues note lists only trade purchases [S3].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate
assumptions.basis: Nil at the SGER level: iuran produksi is the mine owner's obligation and is embedded in the procurement price; the FY2025 cost-of-revenues note carries no royalty or PNBP line [S3].

assumptions.label: Non-coal revenue
assumptions.basis: Nickel, oil palm, sand & limestone, petroleum coke, palm-kernel shell, wood pellets and the hydrogen-peroxide project. FY2025 non-coal revenue was Rp1,799bn [S3] and H1-2026 already Rp1,159bn (sand & limestone Rp495bn, petroleum coke Rp379bn, nickel Rp284bn) [S16]; the forecast annualises the H1 run-rate and adds the Merak hydrogen-peroxide plant [S10] and the Japan wood-pellet contract that management is building as the post-coal growth engine.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on non-coal revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025: total gross profit Rp536.9bn less coal gross profit Rp401.9bn = Rp135.0bn on Rp1,799bn of non-coal revenue = 7.5% [S3].

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation of fixed assets Rp16.01bn plus right-of-use depreciation Rp1.73bn = Rp17.74bn [S2] on a traded book of ~5.3 Mt = ~Rp3.3m per thousand tonnes. Small because the group capitalises mining assets that are still 'mines under development' and therefore not yet depreciated [S3].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining only. The FY2025 investing outflow of Rp475bn [S3] was growth - mining assets, the Tujuh Bara Sejahtera KSO and a Rp30bn subsidiary acquisition - so it is held out of the steady state and carried in capex_other instead. ~Rp8.0m per thousand tonnes funds barging/port equipment and IT for a trading book.

assumptions.label: Expansion capex
assumptions.basis: Tapering allowance for the announced expansion pipeline - the Merak hydrogen-peroxide plant [S10], wood-pellet capacity and mining-asset build-out - scaled from the FY2025 actual spend of Rp505bn on fixed assets, subsidiaries and intangibles [S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at ~30%, at the FY2023-FY2025 average [S0]: the trading model is advance-heavy (Rp3,476bn of advances to suppliers at 31 Dec 2025 [S3]), so a revenue recovery pulls a large cash outflow into working capital.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The LK's own effective rate (tax/PBT) for the last actual year: FY2025 tax expense Rp30.47bn on PBT Rp238.26bn = 12.8% [S3], which is the rate the LK shows being paid and the anchor the house method sets FY+1 to. The FY2023-FY2025 pack average of 17.0% [S0] is dragged up by FY2024's 19.3%; the LK shows 21.0% (FY2022), 19.0% (FY2023), 19.3% (FY2024) and 12.8% (FY2025), so FY2025 is the lowest of the four years and the one the method's last-actual rule takes; the model is not made more cautious than the LK here. A large part of the FY2025 rate comes from final-taxed income at the parent (Rp115.31bn of 'pendapatan yang telah dikenakan pajak final', leaving taxable income of only Rp24.69bn), disclosed in the tax reconciliation [S3 note 22d].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt
assumptions.basis: The P&L interest rate (interest_expense = opening debt x this input): FY2025 interest expense of Rp151.2bn on average gross debt of Rp1,776bn is 8.5% [S0, S3]; the Rp273.64bn Series A bond carried a 10.0% coupon and Series B 10.75% [S6], bracketing the rate. This is NOT the WACC's pre-tax cost of debt, which the engine takes from a separate house build (rupiah rf + corporate debt spread = 9.45%); the two rates are different inputs for different jobs and neither overrides the other.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Set at 2.5%: cash is held as working capital and restricted time deposits pledged against bank facilities [S3], so it earns close to the deposit rate rather than the 10% bond coupon.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No external forecast. The Rp273.64bn Series A bond was repaid at maturity on 25 Oct 2026 from internal cash [S6, S10] and only the Rp9.46bn Series B remains, so gross debt amortises rather than grows.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating item is disclosed; FY2025's small positive other income is not forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Set to zero: the minorities' share was negative (-Rp5.5bn in FY2025) and immaterial to group profit [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Set below the FY2023-FY2024 record: the board declared no dividend for FY2025 after net profit fell 68% [S0, S2], and with operating cash flow negative (-Rp197bn [S3]) and working capital absorbing the recovery, a partial resumption at 15% of earnings is the most likely path.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No issue announced; 15,586.9m shares outstanding [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: IDR long-run inflation of 3.28% [macro deck m.cpi_id] plus a small real premium for a diversified energy-trading franchise; below the 4% house default because the coal book is in structural decline.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set just above the H1-2026 ratio rather than the inflated FY2025 one: SG&A was Rp106bn on Rp4,328bn of H1-2026 revenue (2.5%) against 3.6% for FY2025 [S0], the absolute cost base being roughly fixed around Rp200bn a year with only 65 staff [S2].

challenges.challenge: The primary method is a commodity_producer life-of-asset DCF run with no terminal value (model valuation.methods.dcf_life.tv_share = 0.0) on a business that owns no depleting mine or field — its only mining is the 2 Mt Tujuh Bara Sejahtera KSO [S18] and its traded book is bought-in, not extracted. The card's engine (NAV = sum of life-of-asset DCF per mine/field) presupposes a depleting asset this name does not have, so applying the no-terminal-value frame sets the post-FY2045 value of a going-concern merchant to zero — the report's own words call it "deliberately conservative for a merchant whose franchise could in principle outlive its coal book". This is the wrong method for the industry and it is the whole target: adding a terminal value at the stated terminal_growth of 3.5% roughly doubles the DCF value (from ~Rp57 toward ~Rp105), lifting the base toward Rp90 and the weighted target toward Rp120.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the primary as a going-concern valuation with an explicit terminal value at the sourced rupiah long-run growth rate (in.terminal_growth 3.5% [S0, macro deck m.cpi_id]); the mandated no-terminal-value life-of-asset DCF is retained as a floor at half the DCF weight and the understatement it imposes on a merchant is stated explicitly in section 4. The industry-default 0.6 life-of-asset weight is split 0.4 dcf_fcff / 0.2 dcf_life, justified in qc_justifications.weights.changed; the going-concern run now carries most of its value in terminal value.

challenges.challenge: The core variant view inverts VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL step 1: "A name re-rating WITH the complex while its own P&L is flat is complex alpha to capture, not an 'expensive on its own numbers' kill." SGER's shares ran from Rp240 to Rp840 with the coal complex [S0] and the report kills precisely on "SGER's own profit and loss has not followed it". The report acknowledges the rule but disposes of it with an unsourced assertion ("a merchant's thin spread cannot carry a producer's re-rating").
challenges.answer: The complex-alpha rule is re-tested as the card directs, and SGER does not show the P&L gearing the rule presumes. The card requires re-setting the through-cycle marker when the complex moves and re-testing the name: the model runs on the desk's through-cycle Newcastle path (falling toward the deck's long-run marker), not spot, and the rating is re-tested against that path. The sourced evidence for the exemption is the spread band: coal revenue/cost of revenues F4/F35 = Rp12,217.6bn/Rp11,170.4bn (FY2023), F5/F34 = Rp14,209.1bn/Rp13,225.9bn (FY2024) and F6/F7 = Rp4,940.4bn/Rp4,538.5bn (FY2025) - a high-single-digit percent spread held through the whole commodity cycle. A merchant's pass-through spread does not widen with the benchmark, so a complex re-rating is producer alpha, not a merchant's.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative states "the non-coal lines (nickel, sand & limestone, hydrogen peroxide, wood pellets) scale faster than we assume" (assumptions scenarios.bull), but the bull scenario shocks only d.coal.newc, a.volume and a.cost_per_bcm — other_revenue is never shocked, and other_margin is fixed at 7.5%. The stated bull driver is therefore not in the bull model; all the scenario convexity the report leans on (bull Rp220) comes from coal alone. The non-coal lines are worth ~nothing in the DCF despite being the stated growth engine [S3, S10, S16].
challenges.answer: The stated bull driver is now in the bull model: scenarios.bull adds a.other_revenue x1.2 and scenarios.bear adds a.other_revenue x0.8, alongside the coal/volume/cost shocks, so the non-coal line is shocked in both tails. Section 5 states the mirrored four-driver shock set.

challenges.challenge: SGER funds and operates an IUP OP mine under the Tujuh Bara Sejahtera KSO, taking the sale proceeds against a guaranteed 2,000,000 MT at cumulative stripping ratio 7 [S18, F22/F23] — that is a producer's margin on up to 2 Mt, not a trading spread. The model nonetheless sets strip_ratio 1.0, fuel_share 0, royalty 0 and prices the entire 5.2 Mt at 92% of ASP, i.e. treats KSO tonnes as bought-in. The report calls the mining side "real but small" and gives it no distinct economics.
challenges.answer: The KSO is an operational-cooperation over PT Tujuh Bara Sejahtera's IUP OP, not owned production: SGER funds and operates it and the LK reports it inside the trading figure with no separate mining-segment revenue or mining gross margin [S3]. The 2,000,000 MT is the agreement's guaranteed project quantity, not an annual run-rate [F22], so there is no sourced producer margin to apply to it; the group's mining assets are still mines under development and undepreciated [S3]. Applying a producer margin would invent an unsourced cost, so the KSO stays within the calibrated trading spread and the point is disclosed in section 1 (strip_ratio basis).

challenges.challenge: The Rp3,476bn supplier-advance book — more than half of FY2025 revenue and the audit report's key matter [S3, F13] — is the report's own "single best test", yet the earnings screen stops at a qualitative note and states related-party balances are "small" from a single Rp169.9bn other-payable line [S3]. EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS step 4 requires related-party flows quantified as % of revenue/assets, and step 1 flags an accruals ratio "comfortably above" 10% with three years of negative cash conversion. The bear case assumes the advances always convert.
challenges.answer: Quantified rather than waved away. Related-party other payables are F30 Rp169.9bn = F32 5.18% of total liabilities; the significant portion of the F13 Rp3,475.7bn supplier-advance book is F31 Rp3,301.1bn to third parties for coal and nickel purchases, so the advances are not a related-party channel [S3]. The accruals screen (three-year ratio above 10%, three years of negative cash conversion) is stated in section 3. The bear case is not sized for a write-down because no default, delinquency or impairment is disclosed [S3]; modelling one would be unsourced, so the tractable bear risk (smaller book, narrower spread) is what the scenario carries and advance conversion is named as the signpost.

challenges.challenge: The card step 4 says Indonesian coal realised price keys off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle; the model's benchmark is d.coal.newc and the FY2026E realised price is US$65.76/t. SGER's stated product is ~4,800 kcal/kg GAR (48GAR) [S13, F3], which sits in the deck's HBA III bucket (spot US$45.53) while US$65.76 is essentially the deck's HBA II (spot US$66.1) [deck.coal.hba_ii/hba_iii]. Either the grade assumption or the realisation is off, and the model never reconciles to the HBA series it is supposed to key off.
challenges.answer: Reconciled to the HBA ladder in section 2. SGER's stated product is about F3 4,800 kcal/kg GAR, which clears between HBA II (4,100 kcal/kg GAR) and HBA I (5,300 kcal/kg GAR) on the deck's grade ladder [S25]; it is above the 4,100 grade, not in the HBA III (3,400 kcal/kg) tranche. FY2026E realised price sits just under the HBA II print and below the mid-point of the two rungs its grade straddles [S25], so the realisation is consistent with - slightly conservative against - the ladder. The benchmark series remains the deck's newc because that is the only coal series with a forecast path, with the realisation calibrated on SGER's own disclosed cargoes [S13, S17, S18].

challenges.challenge: The model holds tax at 17.0% while the LK's last actual (FY2025) effective rate is 12.8% [S3; assumptions tax_rate.basis]. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE says tax and royalty rates are the ones the LK shows being paid; using a 3-year average rather than the last actual is a downward drift with no source for why FY2026+ reverts up.
challenges.answer: Tax set to the LK's last-actual effective rate: FY2025 tax expense Rp30.47bn on PBT Rp238.26bn = 12.79% [S3], carried for FY2026E-FY2030E and lt, replacing the pack's 17.0% three-year average. The reconciliation explains the low rate (Rp115.31bn final-taxed income at the parent, taxable income Rp24.69bn [S3 note 22d]).

challenges.challenge: FY2026E volume of 5.2 Mt is stated to be anchored on H1-2026 coal revenue of Rp3,160bn [S16] and "our estimate of the historical half-year split". The disclosed H1 share of the year is ~60% (H1-2025 revenue Rp4,050bn of FY2025 Rp6,739.5bn [S6, S2]); applying 60% to the implied H1 volume (≈2.7 Mt at the model's US$65.76/t realised price and FY2026E FX of 17,570) gives ≈4.6 Mt, not 5.2 Mt. The 5.2 Mt therefore embeds a second-half recovery (~13% above the stated anchor) with no source.
challenges.answer: FY2026E volume cut to 4.6 Mt, the anchored value: H1-2026 coal segment revenue Rp3,160bn [S16] converted at the calibrated realisation and the deck FX gives about 2.7 Mt for the half; the historical first-half share is ~60% (H1-2025 revenue Rp4,050bn of FY2025 Rp6,739.5bn [S2, S6]), giving ~4.6 Mt for the year. The prior 5.2 Mt embedded an unsourced ~13% H2 recovery; growth now comes only from the rebuilt export book (Coalimex, VIMC, Bangladesh) at ~5% p.a., never returning to the FY2024 peak.

challenges.challenge: The equity value renders as "IDR13,093,003,927,920.0bn" (fund record lines 9 and 51: {{mkt.mcap_idr|money}}) — raw rupiah with a "bn" suffix; the true market cap is Rp13,093bn (Rp840 [S0] × 15,586.9m shares). A reader cannot use the number, and it is the figure the whole "pays Rp13.1tn for the equity" argument rests on.
challenges.answer: Market cap now renders with the idrb format: the mcap_idr placeholder prints as IDR13,093bn (~Rp13.1tn) instead of raw rupiah with a bn suffix, in the summary and section 4.

challenges.challenge: The report renders the workforce as "83 people" while the source cited around it, the FY2025 annual report [S2], states 65 employees (and the FY2025 LK [S3] states 83 for 2025 and 85 for 2024). The assumptions opex_pct basis cites "65 staff [S2]" — the two files disagree on the headcount and the report does not say which it used.
challenges.answer: Headcount inconsistency removed: section 1 now states the two documents give different counts (S2 65, S3 83) and relies on the payroll cost rather than a single figure [S2, S3]. The opex_pct basis cites the S2 count.

challenges.challenge: Source S7 is recorded as "SGER non-coal, laba Rp500bn target (IDNFinancials)" but its URL and fetched text [S7] are an IDNFinancials article on foreign buying of BUMI/GOTO — it contains no SGER content and no Rp500bn target. It is uncited in the report, but a mis-titled/mis-URL'd source in the pack undermines the source register.
challenges.answer: The mis-titled/mis-URL'd S7 (an IDNFinancials article on foreign buying of BUMI/GOTO, no SGER content) has been removed from the source register (fund record); it was uncited in the report, so no citation depends on it.

missing_bull_case.note: The non-coal engines (nickel, sand & limestone, petroleum coke, and the Merak hydrogen-peroxide plant) are real, growing (H1-2026 non-coal Rp1,159bn vs FY2025 Rp1,799bn [S3, S16]) and carry differing margins (sand 24.7%, nickel 5.7% [S3]), yet they are modelled at a single 7.5% margin inside a DCF that gives them no terminal value. The KSO mine's producer economics are likewise absent.

missing_bear_case.note: The biggest balance-sheet item — Rp3,476bn of supplier advances (audit key matter [S3]) — is not tested for related-party routing or for non-conversion; the report calls related-party balances "small" from one Rp169.9bn line [S3] without quantifying flows per EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS step 4. The realised-price-over-HBA-ladder risk is also absent.

assumption_realism.note: Volume 5.2 Mt FY2026E does not reconcile to the stated H1 anchor on the historical half-year split; realised price US$65.76/t sits near the deck's HBA II (spot 66.1) not HBA III (spot 45.53) for a ~4,800 kcal/kg GAR product [S13]; tax is 17% against the LK's last-actual 12.8% [S3].

flags.message: cannot re-price the last actual year: volume FY2025A
flags.justification: SGER discloses traded coal tonnage only to FY2023 (7.5 Mt in FY2022 and 10.0 Mt in FY2023 [S13]); the FY2024 and FY2025 LKs give coal segment revenue but no tonnes [S3, S18], so FY+1 cannot be re-priced on a last-actual volume and the forecast volume is instead anchored on the H1-2026 coal revenue of Rp3.16tn at the calibrated realisation [S16].

flags.message: a.cost_per_bcm moves -29% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2045E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: A coal trader's unit cost IS the market price of the coal it buys, so it must track the benchmark rather than stay flat in real terms: the FY2025 cost of revenues fell 54.80% against a 54.35% revenue fall [S2], and the series is built to hold the FY2025 realised margin of ~8% of ASP [S3], which is the last actual's economics.

flags.message: a flat royalty overrides the licence schedule: justify it with the LK's effective rate
flags.justification: SGER pays no iuran produksi at its own level: it is a wholesale coal trader and the FY2025 cost-of-revenues note carries no royalty or PNBP line [S3], the production royalty being borne by the mine owner inside the procurement price; the only mining activity is the KSO over PT Tujuh Bara Sejahtera's IUP OP [S18].

flags.message: expected return -89%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return comes from three sourced drivers, not from a stacked bear case. First, the market pays Rp13.1tn for the equity while our through-cycle EBITDA is a few hundred billion rupiah, an EV/EBITDA in the twenties, because the FY2025 coal book collapsed to Rp4,940bn of revenue from Rp14,209bn and the traded spread that produced FY2024's Rp659bn profit is gone [S3, S18]. Second, the reverse DCF shows the price needs a Newcastle benchmark near US$167/t, about 1.4x the desk's FY2027E benchmark of US$118/t (deck.coal.newc.FY2027E) and about 1.6x its long-run marker of US$105/t (deck.coal.newc.lt), to be justified [S23]. Third, operating cash flow has been negative for three years against positive reported profit, so the earnings the multiple is applied to are not converting to cash [S3].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.15}
flags.justification: The COAL industry card's primary is the no-terminal-value life-of-asset DCF (dcf_life), which suits a depleting producer; SGER owns no depleting mine (its only mining is the 2 Mt Tujuh Bara Sejahtera KSO [S18, F22]) and its non-coal lines (nickel, sand & limestone, hydrogen peroxide, wood pellets) are a growing going concern [S3, S10, S16], so the industry-default 0.6 weight on dcf_life would set the post-horizon value of a merchant to zero. The 0.6 DCF weight is split equally between the mandated dcf_life (floor) and a going-concern dcf_fcff with a terminal value at the sourced IDR long-run rate, so the target reflects the franchise's continuing value; the two cross-checks keep their industry weights.
